I will come back to you with a position on both by Wednesday so we stay on track for Thursday.

Hi Dana,

The four week pilot wrapped on Friday and I pulled the numbers this morning.

Weekly active users on the Acme workspace went 11, 17, 24, 31. Average time to resolve a ticket in the pilot team dropped from 2.3 days to 1.4. The team lead said she would be upset if we took it away, which is the best signal I have.

I want to take this to our VP of Ops next week and ask for 40 seats across two teams. For that I need a pricing proposal from you: per seat cost at 40, what an annual commitment does to it, and whether onboarding is included. Can you get me something by Friday?

Elena

I am in procurement at Globex and I am working with Elena Ruiz on the Acme engagement. Before we can move from pilot to a paid contract, our vendor process requires a completed security questionnaire.

Patricia Gomez

threads.subject: How the best PMs run discovery

messages.body:
The Product Weekly, issue 212

This week: how the best PMs run discovery.

We interviewed product leads at eight companies between 20 and 200 people about how they decide what to build next. Three patterns showed up everywhere.

1. They talk to customers on a schedule, not when they have a question. Five conversations a week was the median.
2. They write the problem down before the solution, and share the problem write-up with engineering before any mockup exists.
3. They kill more than they ship. The best teams had a graveyard doc and were proud of it.

Full piece on the site, about an 8 minute read.

Also this week: a template for a one page problem brief, and a reader question about pricing experiments.

You are receiving this because you subscribed at productweekly.news. Unsubscribe any time from the link below.

summary.summary: A newsletter from The Product Weekly, issue 212, on how strong product teams run customer discovery. Key points: talk to customers on a fixed schedule, write the problem before the solution, and maintain a graveyard of killed ideas. It is a general 8-minute read, not a message to you personally.

messages.body:
Seed Signals, October round-up

Round sizes are up and round counts are down. Median seed in our tracked set was $3.4M this month, against $2.9M in October last year, with about 15% fewer deals closed.

What founders are telling us:

Term sheets are taking longer. The median from first meeting to signed term sheet was 41 days, up from 33.

Pro rata is back on the table. Two thirds of the term sheets we saw this month included some form of pro rata rights, and about a quarter extended them past the next round. Push back on that one if you can.

Option pools are being negotiated harder, with 10% post-money still the most common ask.

On the site this week: a founder's annotated term sheet, and a comparison of three data room tools.

Seed Signals is free. Forward it to a founder who needs it!

Unsubscribe from the link below.

summary.summary: Seed Signals' October newsletter says median seed rounds rose to $3.4M while deal counts fell about 15%. Term sheets now take a median 41 days, pro rata rights are common, and 10% option pools remain the usual ask.

threads.subject: Stack Notes #148: the cost of a flaky test suite

messages.body:
Stack Notes, issue 148

The cost of a flaky test suite

We instrumented CI at six companies for a month. Average time lost to re-running flaky tests was 4.2 engineer hours per week per team, or about one engineer in ten doing nothing. Fixing the top 5% of flaky tests eliminated 80% of the retries.

Also in this issue:

A short write-up on moving a 40-service deployment from cron-based jobs to a queue, including what broke.

Postgres connection pooling for serverless, with the numbers on what a 6 connection cap actually means at load.

A reader's checklist for interviewing senior engineers that does not involve a whiteboard.

Read online or reply with topics you want covered.

Unsubscribe from the link below.

summary.summary: Stack Notes issue 148, a newsletter about the cost of flaky test suites. It reports that flaky tests cost about 4.2 engineer hours per team weekly, and fixing the top 5% removed 80% of retries. Other items cover a queue migration, serverless Postgres pooling, and senior engineer interviews.
summary.ask: Reply with topics you want covered, or read online.

I signed up for Acme last week to take a look (nice product) and noticed the onboarding emails stop after day 2. Was that on purpose?

At GrowthLoop we write onboarding and lifecycle email for B2B products. Typical result for a team your size is a 20 to 35% lift in week two activation, and we can usually show a before and after within a month.

I put together three quick ideas for your day 3 to day 14 sequence. Would you like me to send them over? No cost, no strings, just curious whether it is useful.

Alex Kim
GrowthLoop

summary.ask: Reply if you want the three free onboarding ideas sent.

Dear Dana,

I am the program chair for Umbrella Summit, which takes place March 12 to 13 in Austin. About 1,400 people attend, mostly engineers and engineering leaders at companies under 500 people.

We are putting together a track on building small, senior engineering teams, and your name came up twice when I asked speakers who else we should hear from. I would like to invite you to give a 30 minute talk on how Acme hires and runs its engineering team.

We cover travel and two nights of hotel. There is no fee either way, we do not pay speakers and we do not charge them.

The program locks on November 15. If you are interested, a one paragraph abstract by then is all I need.

Warm regards,
Nadia Hassan
Program Chair, Umbrella Summit

threads.subject: Advice from a student who read your post

messages.body:
Hello Ms. Reyes,

I am a third year computer science student at Northfield University. I read your post about leaving a large company to start Acme and it has stuck with me for weeks.

I am trying to decide between a big company internship next summer and joining a five person startup that a friend's older brother runs. Everyone I ask gives me the answer that matches their own path. I would really value 15 minutes of yours, by email or call, whichever is easier, to hear how you would think about it.

I understand you are busy and will not be offended by a no.

Thank you for reading this,
Aisha Bello

summary.summary: Aisha Bello, a third-year computer science student at Northfield University, is weighing a big company summer internship against joining a five-person startup. She read your post about leaving a large company and asks for 15 minutes to hear how you would think about it, by email or call, and says a no is fine.

threads.subject: Partnership between Wonka Labs and Acme

messages.body:
Hi Dana,

I lead partnerships at Wonka Labs. We make a workflow engine used by about 300 mid-market operations teams, and several of them have asked us whether we integrate with Acme.

I think there is a natural fit: Acme as the front end for the team, Wonka running the automations behind it. We have done two integrations like this in the past year and both drove meaningful signups for the partner.

Would you be open to a 30 minute call to explore it? I can bring our integration lead and a short deck on what the previous two looked like.

Best regards,
Yusuf Demir
Head of Partnerships, Wonka Labs

summary.summary: Yusuf Demir, Head of Partnerships at Wonka Labs, proposes a partnership where Acme serves as the front end and Wonka's workflow engine runs the automations. He cites about 300 mid-market customers asking for an integration and two past partner integrations that drove signups.
summary.ask: A 30-minute call to explore the integration partnership.

threads.subject: Pilot at Hooli: proposal and timeline

messages.body:
Dana,

Thanks for the demo on Tuesday. The platform team is interested in a pilot. Before I take it upstairs I need to understand what a pilot looks like with Acme: how many seats, how long, what it costs, and what you would need from us.

Send me whatever you usually send and I will get it in front of my VP.

Richard

Richard Hale
Director, Platform Operations, Hooli

Richard,

Great to hear. Here is how we usually run a pilot:

Scope: one team, 10 to 15 seats, 4 weeks. Globex and Vandelay both ran it this way.
Cost: free for the pilot. If you convert, the pilot month counts toward the first year.
From you: one champion on your side (I assume that is you), a kickoff call, and a 30 minute check-in each week.
Success criteria: we agree on two numbers up front, usually time to resolve and weekly active users, and we review them together at the end.

I can have a one page pilot agreement to you tomorrow. Which team were you thinking of starting with, and when could they kick off?

Dana

summary.summary: Richard Hale, Director of Platform Operations at Hooli, follows up after Tuesday's demo. Hooli's platform team wants a pilot and he needs seats, duration, cost, and what Acme needs from Hooli before taking it to his VP.
summary.ask: Send your standard pilot proposal covering seats, duration, cost, and requirements.
